name: MathlibAnnex.Piola.divergence_componentFlux_eq_det_sub
title: A component flux gives a determinant difference

content.display_title: A component flux gives a determinant difference
content.one_sentence_role: Expresses the change from one output-coordinate perturbation as a divergence.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$, let $\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Let $e_j$ be the $j$th standard coordinate vector and let $A$ denote an arbitrary real $n\times n$ matrix. Write $g_k(x)=(g(x))_k$ and
$$C_i(A)_j=\det(A[i\leftarrow e_j^{\mathsf T}]).$$
Define the perturbed map and its flux by
$$\begin{aligned}
g^{(i)}(x)&=g(x)+\varphi(x)e_i,\\
V(x)&=\varphi(x)C_i(Dg(x)),\qquad V_j(x):=(V(x))_j=\varphi(x)C_i(Dg(x))_j.
\end{aligned}$$
Then, for every $x$,
$$\operatorname{div}V(x):=\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_jV_j(x)
=\det Dg^{(i)}(x)-\det Dg(x).$$
content.assumptions: The differentiability assumptions are exactly $C^2$ on $g$ and $C^1$ on $\varphi$. The row $i$ and point $x$ are arbitrary. Compact support and invertibility are not required for this pointwise identity.
content.conclusion: The determinant increment is the divergence of the explicitly defined vector field $V$. If $\varphi$ has compact topological support, then so does $V$: with $\operatorname{supp}w:=\overline{\{x:w(x)\ne0\}}$, one has $\operatorname{supp}V\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. This separate support consequence is what permits the subsequent integration.
content.proof_summary: Apply the product rule, cancel the cofactor divergence by Piola, and recognize the remaining sum as a row-replacement determinant.

proof_steps.text:
Put $A=Dg(x)$ and let $d\varphi$ be the row with entries $\partial_j\varphi(x)$. Coordinate vectors satisfy $v=\sum_jv_je_j$, and determinant multilinearity in one row consequently gives
$$\det(A[i\leftarrow v])=\sum_jv_jC_i(A)_j.$$
The finite-sum row-expansion lemmas justify this identity without an invertibility assumption.

The cofactor field is $C^1$: it is a polynomial in the entries of $Dg$, which is $C^1$ because $g$ is $C^2$. The product derivative is therefore valid, and Piola supplies its zero term:
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{div}V(x)&=\sum_j\partial_j\varphi(x)C_i(A)_j+\varphi(x)\sum_j\partial_j(C_i(Dg))_j(x)\\&=\sum_j\partial_j\varphi(x)C_i(A)_j=\det(A[i\leftarrow d\varphi]).\end{aligned}$$

Differentiation gives $Dg^{(i)}(x)=A+e_i\,d\varphi$, whose row $i$ is $A_i+d\varphi$ and whose other rows agree with $A$. By linearity in that row,
$$\det Dg^{(i)}(x)=\det A+\det(A[i\leftarrow d\varphi]).$$
Subtract $\det A$ and insert the previous expression for the divergence. For the later support assertion, $\varphi(x)=0$ implies $V(x)=0$, so the support of $V$ is contained in that of $\varphi$; taking closures preserves the inclusion.

content.lean_realization_notes: Only the $i$th output coordinate changes, so only row $i$ of the derivative matrix changes. The row convention for the cofactor is essential to the identity.
